content: Male sterilization (vasectomy) and female sterilization (tubal ligation) are permanent contraceptive methods. Recommendations for these procedures depend on the context and the scope of practice of the healthcare provider. Some methods are recommended outright, while others are considered appropriate only under specific circumstances or within the context of rigorous research. Certain methods may also fall outside the typical scope of practice, with evidence not yet assessed. All recommendations assume that healthcare workers offering these services will receive task-specific training beforehand. Implementing task-sharing strategies requires effective systems for monitoring, supervision, and referral. The options are inclusive and do not favor or exclude any specific type of provider. The choice of healthcare worker for a specific task depends on local needs and conditions. Family planning methods and services are typically offered by various types of providers, as specified by national policies and service delivery guidelines. These providers include lay health workers, pharmacy workers, pharmacists, auxiliary nurses, nurse-midwives, nurses, advanced clinicians, and doctors. The World Health Organization (WHO) provides recommendations on which cadres of providers can safely offer specific family planning services. Contraceptive services include informed choice counseling, combined oral contraceptives (COCs), progestin-only pills (POPs), emergency contraceptive pills (ECPs), fertility awareness methods (e.g., Standard Days Method, TwoDay Method), lactational amenorrhea method (LAM), condoms (male and female), diaphragms, spermicides, injectables (e.g., DMPA, NET-EN), implants, intrauterine devices (IUDs), vasectomy, and tubal ligation. The appropriateness of these methods varies depending on the provider's training and the healthcare setting. All recommendations emphasize the importance of confidentiality, particularly when dealing with sensitive information. This is especially critical for adolescents or individuals who may face judgment or stigma. Healthcare workers, such as nurses and midwives, play a key role in family planning services. They provide counseling, assess medical eligibility, and help clients select appropriate contraceptive methods. For instance, a nurse may counsel a breastfeeding mother on the use of progestin-only pills (POPs) or discuss long-term options like injectables or IUDs. Similarly, an adolescent seeking emergency contraception may receive counseling on both short-term and long-term contraceptive methods, with an emphasis on dual protection (e.g., condoms and oral contraceptives) to prevent both pregnancy and sexually transmitted infections (STIs). The process of providing family planning services involves several steps, including client registration, counseling, service provision, and follow-up. Counseling involves discussing reproductive intentions, assessing risks, and helping clients make informed choices. Service provision includes administering the chosen contraceptive method and providing instructions for its use. Follow-up appointments are scheduled to monitor the client’s experience and address any concerns. Digital tools and systems can enhance the delivery of family planning services by automating data collection, decision support, and reminders. For example, electronic systems can send SMS reminders to clients about upcoming appointments or follow-ups, ensuring continuity of care. These tools also support healthcare workers by providing decision-making prompts and ensuring that key data elements are recorded. In summary, family planning services require a structured approach involving trained healthcare workers, effective systems for monitoring and referral, and a commitment to client confidentiality and informed choice. The integration of digital tools can further improve service delivery and client outcomes.
